title: Acids and alkalis
ks3: Chemical reactions: acids, alkalis and neutralisation
intro: From lemon juice to soap: learn the pH scale, indicators and how acids and alkalis cancel each other out.
description: Free KS3 Chemistry questions with answers on acids and alkalis: the pH scale, universal indicator and litmus, everyday acids and alkalis, and neutralisation. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9.

questions.q: On the pH scale, what does pH 7 mean?
questions.hint: 7 is right in the middle of the scale from 0 to 14.
questions.explain: pH 7 is neutral: neither acid nor alkali. Pure water is pH 7.

questions.q: A substance has a pH of 2. What is it?
questions.explain: Below 7 is acidic, and the lower the number the stronger the acid. pH 2 is a strong acid.
Lemon juice contains citric acid. Sour taste is a sign of an acid (but never taste chemicals in the lab!).

questions.q: Which pH is the strongest alkali?
questions.explain: Above 7 is alkaline, and the higher the number the stronger the alkali. pH 13 is the strongest here.

questions.q: Which of these is an alkali?
questions.explain: Oven cleaner is a strong alkali. Vinegar, lemon juice and cola are all acids.

questions.q: Why do strong acids and alkalis carry a hazard warning sign?
options: They are corrosive and can damage skin and eyes
questions.hint: What would a strong acid do to your skin?
questions.explain: Strong acids and alkalis are corrosive: they can burn skin and damage eyes. That's why we wear goggles.

options: A substance that changes colour in acids and alkalis
questions.explain: An indicator changes colour to show whether something is acidic, neutral or alkaline.

questions.q: Universal indicator turns red in a solution. What does that tell you?
questions.hint: Red is at the low end of the pH colour chart.
questions.explain: Red means a strong acid (about pH 1 to 3). Green is neutral and purple is a strong alkali.

questions.q: What colour is universal indicator in a neutral solution?
questions.hint: It's in the middle of the rainbow of colours.

questions.q: Blue litmus paper is dipped into a liquid and turns red. What is the liquid?
questions.hint: Litmus: acids turn blue litmus red.
questions.explain: Acids turn blue litmus red. Alkalis turn red litmus blue. Litmus only tells you acid or alkali, not the exact pH.

questions.q: Red cabbage juice can be used as an indicator. Why?
options: It changes colour depending on pH
questions.explain: Red cabbage contains a dye that changes colour as the pH changes, so it works as a natural indicator.

questions.q: What happens when an acid and an alkali are mixed in the right amounts?
questions.explain: They react and cancel each other out: this is neutralisation. The pH moves towards 7.

questions.q: Finish the word equation: acid + alkali → salt + …
questions.hint: Neutralisation makes a salt and a very common liquid.

questions.q: Indigestion is caused by too much stomach acid. How do antacid tablets help?
options: They are bases that neutralise some of the acid
questions.explain: Antacids contain bases that neutralise some of the extra stomach acid, which eases the pain.

questions.q: Alkali is slowly added to an acid with universal indicator in it. Which colour change do you see?
options: Red, then orange, yellow and green
questions.hint: The pH rises from low towards 7.
questions.explain: The pH rises from acidic towards neutral, so the colour goes red → orange → yellow → green. Add too much alkali and it goes blue, then purple.

questions.q: Farmers sometimes spread lime (an alkaline substance) on fields. Why?
options: To neutralise soil that is too acidic
To make the soil more acidic
questions.hint: Most crops grow best at a pH near 7.
questions.explain: Lime neutralises acidic soil so crops grow better.
